title: Pipes and Cisterns
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Pipes and Cisterns. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
Convert completion time into a rate

If a pipe fills a tank in a hours, its rate is 1/a tank per hour. An outlet that empties it in b hours has rate -1/b. Add signed rates while pipes operate together. A positive net rate fills the tank; a negative rate empties it.

For several pipes, use a common time unit and add their rates. If the tank is partly filled, calculate the remaining fraction before dividing by the net rate. These methods assume constant rates and unchanged capacity.

Worked example: Pipes that fill a tank in 6 h and 12 h have combined rate (\(1/6+1/12=1/4\)) tank per hour, so they fill it in 4 h. A 9 h leak changes the net rate to (\(1/4-1/9=5/36\)) tank per hour.

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• Choose one tank as one work unit and write each rate as tanks per hour.
  • Use plus for inlets and minus for outlets or leaks.
  • Find the net rate before calculating time.
  • For alternating operation, calculate work during each interval and update the remaining fraction.
  • Check that the net rate has the correct sign and the time is plausible.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• Filling rate from time t: 1/t tank per unit time.
  • Net rate = sum of inlet rates minus sum of outlet rates.
  • Time = remaining work / positive net rate.
  • Zero net rate means the water level is unchanged.
  • Convert all rates to the same time unit before adding.

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    Two inlets fill a tank in 8 hours and 12 hours. How long do they take together?

    1. (\(4\text{ h}\))
    2. (\(4.8\text{ h}\))
    3. (\(5\text{ h}\))
    4. (\(10\text{ h}\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(4.8\text{ h}\))

    Their combined rate is (\(1/8+1/12=5/24\)) tank per hour. Time (\(=24/5=4.8\)) hours.

  2. Core:

    A pipe fills a tank in 10 hours and a leak empties it in 15 hours. If both are open, when is the tank full?

    1. (\(20\text{ h}\))
    2. (\(25\text{ h}\))
    3. (\(30\text{ h}\))
    4. (\(35\text{ h}\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(30\text{ h}\))

    Net rate (\(=1/10-1/15=1/30\)) tank per hour, so the tank fills in 30 hours.

  3. Foundation:

    Two pipes fill a tank in 6 hours and 12 hours. How long do they take together?

    1. (\(3 h\))
    2. (\(4 h\))
    3. (\(6 h\))
    4. (\(9 h\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(4 h\))

    Combined rate is (\(1/6+1/12=1/4\)) tank per hour, so the tank fills in 4 hours.

  4. Standard:

    A pipe fills a tank in 6 hours and a leak empties it in 9 hours. If both stay open, how long does an empty tank take to fill?

    1. (\(12 h\))
    2. (\(15 h\))
    3. (\(18 h\))
    4. (\(54 h\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(18 h\))

    Net rate is (\(1/6-1/9=1/18\)) tank per hour, so filling takes 18 hours.

  5. Challenge:

    A tank is one-third full. An inlet fills it in 4 hours and an outlet empties it in 12 hours. How long until it is full with both open?

    1. (\(2 h\))
    2. (\(3 h\))
    3. (\(4 h\))
    4. (\(6 h\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(4 h\))

    Remaining work is 2/3 tank. Net rate is (\(1/4-1/12=1/6\)) tank per hour, so time is (\((2/3)/(1/6)=4\)) hours.
